title: Efficient Analysis of Carrier Transport and TM-TE Emission in AlGaN UVC LEDs via Multi-band Localization Landscape Theory
authors: Yu-Ming Chang, Ping-Jie Zhuang, Marcel Filoche, Claude Weisbuch, James S. Speck, Yuh-Renn Wu
abstract: AlGaN-based UVC LEDs (220-250 nm) suffer from poor hole confinement and strain-induced |Z>-band dominance at high Al content (>60%), leading to increased TM emission and reduced external quantum efficiency (EQE). While conventional k.p models combined with Schrodinger, Poisson, and drift-diffusion solvers are widely used to study optical transitions, they are computationally expensive. In this work, we apply the multiband Localization Landscape (LL) model, including the effect of strain, as an alternative that replaces the eigenvalue problem to efficiently capture quantum effects and carrier localization. Using the 3D multi-band LL model with the Wigner-Weyl formalism, we reproduce emission and absorption spectra trends similar to the results in 3D k.p calculations, but with significantly reduced simulation time. The polarization ratio also agrees well with published experimental results across a wide spectral range. Furthermore, we analyze electrical characteristics such as band structure, polarization switching, and carrier confinement under alloy fluctuations and strain. This multi-band LL-based approach provides a fast and reliable solution for understanding and optimizing UVC LED performance.
summary: This work introduces an efficient Multi-band Localization Landscape model to simulate carrier transport in AlGaN UVC LEDs. It overcomes the computational bottleneck of traditional k.p methods by replacing eigenvalue solutions with a landscape approach, while accurately incorporating critical physical effects like strain and alloy disorder. The method provides a fast yet reliable tool for optimizing deep-UV emitter performance.
main_problem: The primary challenge is efficiently modeling carrier transport and emission polarization in AlGaN UVC LEDs, which are complicated by poor hole confinement, strain effects, and random alloy disorder.
main_result: The proposed Multi-band Localization Landscape (LL) model significantly reduces simulation time compared to conventional k.p methods while accurately reproducing spectral trends and polarization ratios across a wide range of conditions.
method: A hybrid approach combining the LL model with the Wigner–Weyl formalism is used within a 3D drift-diffusion framework, replacing computationally expensive eigenvalue problems.
model_or_system: The system is an AlGaN/AlN quantum well structure operating in the deep-UV range. The modeling incorporates strain effects (via piezoelectricity and deformation potential) and random alloy fluctuations to describe carrier localization and transport.
key_observables: Emission and absorption spectra, polarization ratio (TE/TM), band structure evolution, hole/electron current densities, and device electrical characteristics (J-V curves).
important_parameters: High Al content (>60%), compressive strain, alloy fluctuation magnitude, and operating wavelength ($\lambda$ from 223 nm to 294 nm).
main_assumptions: The LL model is assumed to provide an accurate quantum description by replacing the full Schrödinger eigenvalue problem; the framework relies on a self-consistent solution of Poisson and drift-diffusion equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structure transitions based on polarization (TE vs. TM), show how strain modifies the valence band ground state, and compare carrier/current densities with and without the inclusion of strain-induced deformation terms.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem in UVC LEDs, details the limitations of existing k.p methods, proposes the LL model as an efficient alternative, validates its accuracy against full calculations, and applies it to analyze polarization switching and carrier confinement under realistic material stresses.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state devices, the core methodology—using a simplified landscape approach (LL) to capture complex quantum effects (localization, disorder) without solving massive eigenvalue problems—is highly relevant for modeling open quantum systems or strongly interacting many-body physics where full diagonalization is prohibitive.
